title: MB7-22248
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, citizen of India, appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated October 24, 2017, rejecting his claim for refugee protection on the grounds that he would have a safe and reasonable internal flight alternative (IFA) in Mumbai. Allegations
Mr. XXXX is a Sikh XXXX from the state of Uttar Pradesh (UP). He alleged that:

His father and two brothers live on 12 acres of farm land worth about CAD$300,000 belonging to the father. His wife and children live there in a house, nicer than those of his brothers that Mr. XXXX built with his earnings. Normally a father will bequeath his land to his sons in equal portions. Until 2013, however, Mr. XXXX did not plan to ask for a share as, unlike his brothers, he had not worked on the farm.
Mr. XXXX began to do some XXXX XXXX in 2011 after returning from XXXX work in Kenya. By then, his brothers had begun to exhibit jealousy of him.

In 2013, Mr. XXXX asked his father to allocate the land in equal shares to him and his brothers. This upset them. They moved their parents out of Mr. XXXX home, and also demanded that in return he give them 2/3 of his past and present income and house.
The father would have been amenable to Mr. XXXX request, but was caught between the two sides. The Panchayat declined to mediate, saying it was up to the father.

Mr. XXXX elder brother has close ties with Ministers and other politicians from the state-governing Congress Party and also with the UP police. In June 2014, apparently at that brother's behest, the police arrested, tortured, threatened to kill and for two days detained Mr. XXXX on baseless allegations that his Punjabi friend, who had visited him, was a pro-Khalistan anti-national, and that Mr. XXXX had links with and had financially supported such separatists. Police released him on condition that he not shelter pro-Khalistanis and stay away from the part of the family property where his brothers worked.

The brothers told neighbours that this was the beginning and that they would uproot Mr. XXXX from the village. Police again summoned him. Rather than comply, he returned to Kenya in XXXX 2013 to work in a Gurdwara there. The UP police came to his home, telling his wife he had violated their conditions and had joined the militants. His brothers searched for him. The father told her, emotionally, that he was helpless and that the elder brother planned to get Mr. XXXX killed by the police.

Mr. XXXX returned to India in XXXX 2014 because his Kenyan work visa expired. Afraid to go home, he went to a Gurdwara to which he had been referred in Faridabad, Haryana and applied for a position there. When he demurred at their request to be verified by the Haryana police, explaining his past problems and fear of returning to UP, they declined to hire him. Instead, they offered to let him perform religious duties without pay, for room and board, and to receive small donations from congregants. Thereafter, Mr. XXXX wife told him the UP police were frequently questioning her and neighbours about him.

In August 2015, a truck driver from a neighbouring UP village sought overnight shelter at the Faridabad Gurdwara because his truck had broken down. He recognized Mr. XXXX as he had performed a religious rite at the driver's home. A few days later, Mr. XXXX, standing on the balcony above the Gurdwara entrance, spotted his brothers and four unknown men circling the temple in a jeep. (Questioned how he recognized that it was his brothers, he testified that it was an open vehicle.) He informed the Gurdwara president. The latter later told Mr. XXXX that the men had persistently requested to stay in a room in the Gurdwara, but had left after he refused. The president then told Mr. XXXX he must leave the Faridabad Gurdwara because he didn't want trouble.

Mr. XXXX decided that he needed to leave India again as his Faridabad experience taught him relocation in India without police verification was impossible. An 'agent' told him to hide out in Kenya while he arranged a visa to a safe country where Mr. XXXX could live permanently. He went back to Kenya on XXXX XXXX, 2015.

Mr. XXXX returned to India on XXXX XXXX, 2015, after the agent told him he needed his passport to obtain a religious worker visa that had been arranged with an Ontario Gurdwara as sponsor. He went with the agent to the Canadian High Commission in Delhi on November 2, 2015. The visa was issued on November 24, 2015.

To Mr. XXXX surprise and concern, the agent told him he had to delay his departure for Canada because the sponsoring Gurdwara was 'occupied'. Meanwhile, the agent tried unsuccessfully to get him a UK visa. The agent sheltered Mr. XXXX until sending him to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2016.

Mr. XXXX immediately told an official of the Ontario Gurdwara about his problems. The latter assured him he would try to keep Mr. XXXX permanently, but, in the meantime, to perform his religious duties. On August 31, 2016, the official demanded a big donation to keep Mr. XXXX permanently. Mr. XXXX also came to know that the temple management were not willing to keep him on long term. He asked the official for his passport, but he refused and said it would be returned to him at the Toronto airport.

Afraid to return to India, Mr. XXXX sought advice and was told to claim asylum in Montreal even without his passport. He left for Montreal that same day. He filed his claim on October 4, 2016, presenting a photocopy of his passport.
In a later update of his BOC, Mr. XXXX said his elder brother and his goons were receiving help from the police to find him. RPD decision

While the RPD member had some credibility misgivings about Mr. XXXX evidence that he had by chance noticed his brothers driving around the Gurdwara in Faridabad, he found these were outweighed by the otherwise detailed and consistent testimony and the documents corroborating it. He also held that behaviour that might be construed as incompatible with subjective fear (re-availment, delay in claiming) were reasonably explained. He thus accepted that Mr. XXXX had credibly established his main allegations.1
The RPD member's rejection of this claim was based on his findings against Mr. XXXX on both prongs of the IFA test.

When reviewing the RPD decision, I am required to independently determine whether the RPD was correct in relation to each alleged error of law, fact or mixed fact and law. As I find that the RPD had no meaningful advantage in its assessment of the evidence, I have not deferred to it in my analysis of its findings.2
I have read all the documents on file. I have also listened to and closely annotated the audio recording of the RPD hearing. ANALYSIS Section 96 or 97 claim
Appeal counsel appeared to refer to the IRPA sections 96 and 97 tests interchangeably.3

Hearing counsel by contrast, acknowledged that for Mr. XXXX fear of his elder brother, this is an IRPA section 97 claim. I agree, as it is not based on any differences between them related to the five Convention refugee grounds. In the result, Mr. XXXX claim that he faces a risk of death, torture or cruel and unusual treatment at his brother's hand or behest because of their property dispute falls under section 97. He must thus demonstrate that he would probably be so harmed in the proposed IFA.4

Hearing counsel submitted and appeal counsel implied that, due to the element of alleged militant links, this is a section 96 claim vis-à-vis the UP police, on the grounds of political opinion. I disagree. To fall under section 96, the UP police would have to perceive Mr. XXXX, even if wrongly, as having pro-militant or at least 'anti-national' opinions, and to persecute him or be a serious threat to do so for that reason. As explained more fully below under the IFA first prong analysis, in my opinion, the evidence did not establish on the balance of probability that the police in India actually perceived Mr. XXXX, a man with no prior political involvement, as having such opinions. His evidence indicated rather that his arrest and mistreatment by the police on purported militant-linked grounds was a set-up at his elder brother's behest and was unrelated to his real or perceived political views. IFA first prong: safety - RPD correct Did appellant perceive a significant risk that his brother would find and harm him in Mumbai?

When the RPD member first asked whether he could restart his life in Mumbai, Mr. XXXX said it would be very difficult, because upon applying for a position at the Gurdwara there, its officials would ask the Faridabad Gurdwara about him. They would be told about his brothers having gone there to try to kill him. Any Mumbai Gurdwara would then decline to hire him, because he represented trouble and they would get a bad name.5 Asked whether they might in fact understand his situation, he replied that at best this would lead, as it had in Faridabad, to them offering him to stay with no salary and subsisting on minimal donations from persons attending the temple.6

The member asked whether there were other reasons Mr. XXXX would have difficulties in Mumbai. Mr. XXXX said he would not be able to get a Gurdwara post, and could do no other type of work there, both because he had done priestly work for over twenty years and most importantly because he does not speak the local language.7 Asked whether the problems he expected in Mumbai was finding work, he said yes. Would there be other problems? The biggest one would be finding work, reiterated Mr. XXXX. He added that his lack of residence papers should he move to the state containing Mumbai would also stop him from buying land for a house or other purposes or generally from doing anything.8

The RPD member asked whether anything else would prevent Mr. XXXX from settling in Mumbai. Yes, replied Mr. XXXX, were his [elder] brother to come to know, he would go there and kill him.9 The RPD member found that this reason only having been raised on "the third attempt to elicit a complete response" was a strong indication that Mr. XXXX did not perceive it as a significant risk.10 Asked why he thought his brother would find out that he was in Mumbai, Mr. XXXX said that the biggest chance of that happening was that, as in Faridabad, someone would spot him and inform the brother.11 This too, the member wrote, strongly conveyed unlikelihood that the brother would pose a problem to Mr. XXXX if he settled in Mumbai. He added that Mumbai lying over 1,500 km from Mr. XXXX home town made his brother learning he was there through travellers unlikely. For these three reasons, the RPD member concluded that Mr. XXXX had not established that his brother probably has the interest or capacity to seek, find and reach him in Mumbai. He held that Mr. XXXX had thus not established the requisite risk under either IRPA sections 96 or 97.12 Risk of brother harming appellant were he to renounce interest in the family land

Mr. XXXX was then asked what interest his brother would have in harming him were he legally to renounce any claim to their father's land. Even then his brother would not spare him, he explained, because the brother would think that otherwise in two or four years he might change his mind and ask for it back. 13 Earlier, he had testified that his brother would kill him even if he gave up any claim to the land, as the brother was concerned that an eventual change of party in power in UP could lead to Mr. XXXX convincing a governing politician to have the state let him have his land back. The RPD member found that, even factoring in the level of corruption in India, this was too speculative.

The member also stated that, were Mr. XXXX to renounce unequivocally any interest in the family land, his brother would likely be uninterested in spending anymore time, energy or money to pursue him. This, added the member, would be all the more so were Mr. XXXX to give up his house on that land (a further source of jealousy as it was much nicer than those of his brothers). Doing both these things and disappearing to Mumbai, the member concluded, would likely make his brother unable and unwilling to hunt Mr. XXXX down on the remote chance that he eventually resurfaces, changes his mind and tries to undo his renunciation.14
The member added that land ownership is not a fundamental right, so having Mr. XXXX give it up in order to return safely to India would not be unreasonable.15

Appeal counsel submits that the RPD hadn't had to persist to get Mr. XXXX to explain that he feared his brother would kill him because he could try to reclaim his land rights in future, and that he might be discovered in Mumbai the same way as in Faridabad.16 While the appellant acknowledges that chance is involved in the possibility of his being spotted in Mumbai, adds counsel, it was unreasonable, because of the existence of the tenant registration system, to limit that possibility to mere chance.17

The RPD member's first reason, that Mr. XXXX only got round to fear of his brother on the third try and thus does not subjectively view it as a significant risk, is the least important, and probably the weakest. The initial question posed on IFA was whether it would be possible for Mr. XXXX to restart his life in Mumbai.18 This could reasonably have been perceived as a second prong question relating to matters like employment. It is true that he further responded in the same vein to subsequent open-ended questions about problems he might face in Mumbai, but he did then bring up fear of his brother without being explicitly prompted by a question about safety. While it is possible this delay noted by the RPD member was a sort of Freudian slip, or at least an implied admission of low risk, on Mr. XXXX part, in all the circumstances that would in my view be an unsafe and thus incorrect conclusion. In any event, the real issue is whether Mr. XXXX objectively would face the requisite risk of torture or death from his brother were he to try living in Mumbai.

I find the RPD member's other two related reasons, based on the objective unlikelihood of the brother learning of Mr. XXXX presence in Mumbai through a chance spotting there by a mutual acquaintance from back home, correct. The member's reasoning, founded on the vast population of Mumbai and its distance from UP, is cogent. While anything is possible, here it is improbable. In fact I believe there is also not even a serious chance of this coming to pass.
I thus agree with the RPD's finding that there is insufficient risk of Mr. XXXX being discovered in Mumbai through mere chance to warrant protection on that basis.

Would renunciation of any right to a share in the land sufficiently placate the brother? In his BOC, Mr. XXXX wrote that in 2013 his brothers were telling villagers that they would uproot him from the village. Apparently, then, they did not declare, publicly at least, they wanted to kill him. On the other hand, Mr. XXXX wrote that his father said his elder son planned to have him killed through the UP police.19 At that time, however, Mr. XXXX had shown no sign of backing down in what his brothers, rightly or wrongly, viewed as an outrageous demand.

Early in his testimony, Mr. XXXX was asked what motivated his elder brother to want to kill him. He replied that it was because the brother wants to take Mr. XXXX land.20 This also indicates that transformation of that desire to accomplishment, by Mr. XXXX eliminating his claim to the land or transferring it to his brothers or elder brother, would seriously diminish that motivation.

As noted above, Mr. XXXX also asserted that his giving up his right or claim to a one-third share of their father's land would not suffice, as his elder brother would fear that Mr. XXXX might try to retract his renunciation following an eventual change of state government. The RPD member found this too speculative.

Appeal counsel argues that the brothers persecuted Mr. XXXX and have looked for him even though he has not taken any steps to pursue an interest in the land since 2013. Thus, he submits, it is to the contrary speculative to conclude that nothing would happen to the appellant even if he cedes the land.21 Those actions by the brothers, however, took place while Mr. XXXX had taken no steps formally to renounce his interest in the disputed land. What then, would be the effect were he to do so?

The matter would be simpler were Mr. XXXX already the owner of the disputed land. A deed or similar instrument, properly drawn up and registered, transferring his land to the brothers would give them a great deal of assurance that the land had become solely theirs. In such circumstances, the scenario envisaged by the appellant, under which the elder brother is still motivated enough to have him killed to ward off a potential future post-election attempt somehow to cancel the deed would be, as the RPD member found, too speculative to meet the risk threshold required for protection.

My understanding of the evidence, however, is that Mr. XXXX does not yet own the four acres in question. They still belong to his father. The cultural norm is that he would inherit them. He was willing at first not to insist on that, given he hadn't previously worked the land, but later changed his position after doing some farm labour. Whatever right he may have to that land has apparently not vested. Renunciation of that right, in such circumstances, might involve some combination of his father's changing his will, a signed declaration by the appellant, or possibly a formal real estate document that might or might not be registrable on title under UP law. Whether that would become fully effective and irrevocable while the father is still alive I do not know, or have evidence to ascertain. Be that as it may, it would probably mollify the elder brother, given that it is in any event the most he could have asked for at any stage of this affair while the father is still alive. That would be even more so were the appellant's family to vacate their house and join him elsewhere, leaving the brothers in factual control of the property and as much legal control as possible. Risk of UP police coming after appellant in Mumbai

Hearing counsel submitted and appeal counsel argues that there is also sufficient risk of Mr. XXXX coming to grief should the UP police learn that he is in Mumbai. The RPD member noted that Mr. XXXX never mentioned fearing the police would come and get him there. This, he wrote, illustrated that Mr. XXXX himself did not consider this an important risk.22
Nonetheless, both counsel made this argument and I will consider it. Appeal counsel submits that the risk stems from the tenant registration system mandated by law in Mumbai and other Indian cities.

Appeal counsel submitted arguments, based on the contents of the India National Documentation Package at the time of filing the appeal, regarding the risk that Mr. XXXX new location, were he to resettle in Mumbai, would come to the attention of the UP police in his village, and then to his brother, due to the tenant verification systems in that city.

The India NDP has been updated several times since the RPD decision, most recently on May 31, 2019. The updated information there indicates that interstate police connectivity is increasing23 and that, when police do carry out a tenant verification, the process seems to involve their sending the tenant's ID details to the police in his home village. The research information in the most recent NDP, for example, confirms that tenant verification requirements in India could lead the police in one of the proposed IFAs to communicate or cross-check information with the police in UP, and that the verification process is supported by a digital portal, which enables citizens to "seek antecedent verification" of tenants.24 The sources cited in the new Tab 14.8 of the NDP also say that at least in Delhi, the police do send verification forms to the police station where the person previously lived. It is reasonable to assume that this may very well be the case for Mumbai as well.

For the purposes of this decision, then, I am prepared to assume, as appeal counsel argues,25 that police in UP and Mumbai have the capacity to communicate with each other about Mr. XXXX, and that it is probable that his eventual attempt to rent housing for himself and his family would result in an inquiry reaching the UP police in his home village indicating his whereabouts. It is thus not necessary to invite counsel to file further submissions on the updated NDP evidence on these issues.

In my opinion, however, the RPD's conclusion on insufficient police interest in Mr. XXXX remains correct: The UP police, even if notified of Mr. XXXX presence elsewhere in India, are highly unlikely to go get him. Further, my opinion is based on Mr. XXXX own evidence.

As the RPD member noted, even hearing counsel indicated, the UP police appear to have played a facilitator role for the brothers, rather than acting out of any truly held suspicions about Mr. XXXX. They arrested him at the brothers' behest. After mistreating him for two days, and despite having purported during the detention to suspect him of militant links, they released him after two days, apparently without a bribe. There was no evidence that they took any action to have the Punjabi friend who visited Mr. XXXX investigated or arrested. Nor was there evidence that they filed a First Information Report, arrest warrant or charges against Mr. XXXX. He was able to travel to and back from Kenya twice without problem after the dispute with his brothers broke out. And as the RPD member noted, when the brothers were tipped off that Mr. XXXX was at the Gurdwara in Faridabad, Haryana, the UP police neither travelled there to get him nor had the Haryana police arrest him. The brothers were left to attempt to do so themselves. Taking all this into account, in my view the RPD member was correct to find that the UP police have insufficient interest in Mr. XXXX to expend the time and resources to round him up in Mumbai and to bring him back to their village. Police passing on appellant's IFA location to brother

That leaves the possibility that, notified through the tenant registration process of Mr. XXXX location in Mumbai, the UP police would at least pass that information on to Mr. XXXX elder brother. Given their apparent assistance to him in the past, albeit limited to the local level, that seems reasonably possible, even probable.

On Mr. XXXX evidence, however, I do not see more than a mere possibility that this would result in the brother himself killing or torturing Mr. XXXX in Mumbai, or hiring someone to do so. As Mr. XXXX wrote, his father said the brother had plans to get him killed through the police, not at his own hands. Further, the brother has no influence over or impunity from the police in Mumbai, just as he apparently had none in Haryana. In my opinion, the evidence does not establish the requisite risk that the brother would take the necessary risk and trouble to go to Mumbai to commit these serious crimes. This would be even more so were Mr. XXXX to cede his interest in the family land.

In the result, I find that the RPD member was correct in his conclusion that Mr. XXXX had not established that he would suffer a risk to his life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Mumbai, on a balance of probabilities. IFA second prong: reasonableness - RPD correct

As summarized above, Mr. XXXX testified that he would not be able to work as a priest in Mumbai, because the Gurdwaras, after checking with the Faridabad temple, would not want to hire him, at least formally and for pay, for fear of involving themselves in trouble. He also said that this was effectively his only vocation.

Mr. XXXX acknowledged to the RPD member that he would be able to practice his religion in Mumbai as a lay member of the congregation could, though not as a priest.26 Hearing counsel submitted that this would constitute a violation of his fundamental human right to religious expression, rendering Mumbai unreasonable as an IFA.27

The RPD member disagreed with this submission, as well as those regarding the possibility of Mr. XXXX finding other sufficient employment and language barriers. He found that Mr. XXXX had not met the high threshold to establish that Mumbai would be unreasonable as an IFA, namely conditions there that would jeopardize his life or safety.28
Appeal counsel made no submission on the IFA second prong. I agree with the RPD member's conclusion on it.

In any event, I further find it improbable that Mr. XXXX would be unable to find employment as a priest in Mumbai because of his problems with his family. He apparently had a good work record with other Gurdwaras, from which he could obtain references, before Faridabad. The concerns of the Faridabad temple president also did not stop him from obtaining sponsorship and an offer of employment from an Ontario Gurdwara. He must have done this either by explaining to the latter the context of those concerns, or by omitting to mention his stint at the Faridabad temple, where he was not even formally employed. In either case, even if being unable to preach in a Gurdwara might be an unreasonable restriction of Mr. XXXX religious freedom, I find that he did not establish that he would be unable to find a position allowing him to do so.
I thus find that the RPD member was correct to find that Mr. XXXX would have a safe and reasonable IFA in Mumbai.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant XXXX XXXX is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
